answer:
## HYPOTHESIS (deliverable)

**Higher present-oriented financial behaviour is associated with higher adiposity in NLSY79, but the association is largely concurrent rather than prospective — these data support a positive *association* between a savings-based present-orientation proxy and BMI, not a demonstrated causal effect of time preference on weight.**

Stated with the exposure named exactly as what it is: using the 1989 items *"Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview"* (ordered 1 put-more-in < 3 no-change < 2 took-more-out < 4 no-savings as a **savings-based present-orientation proxy**, not a measured discount rate) plus its binary form (dis-saver or no savings) and a net-saving/income ratio, BMI rises monotonically across the four categories — **mean BMI1989 24.54 (saver) → 24.97 (no change) → 25.14 (dis-saver) → 25.50 (no savings); obesity prevalence 10.1% → 11.6% → 13.0% → 15.6%**; r = +0.077, ρ = +0.064, n = 10,410 — and the gradient survives adjustment for age, sex, race cohort, ASVAB, parental education/occupation, family size, 1985 family net wealth and 1989 family income (**TP-ordinal b = +0.230 BMI units/step, SE 0.061, p = 1.6e-4, n = 4,569**; TP_high +0.436, p = 0.001; obesity OR 1.10/step). **Direction is not established:** adding 8-year-lagged BMI1981 removes 54–58% of the coefficient (→ +0.096, p = 0.020), the genuinely prospective BMI1992|BMI1989 model falls to +0.063 (p = 0.082, n = 3,861), and **BMI1981 itself predicts *more* present orientation in 1989 (+0.013/BMI unit, p = 0.003)** — reverse-channel evidence. Effect size: +0.23 BMI/step ≈ 0.05 SD ≈ 0.7 kg; TP_high ≈ 0.09 SD ≈ 1.3 kg.

**Pre-registered positive sign: matches in 54/59 fitted specifications; 100% for every primary exposure** (tp_ord, tp_high, tp_cat3, D_dissav, D_nosav all positive in all designs; save_ratio negative in all 5 as pre-registered). The 5 exceptions are all the "no change" category dummy, which sits slightly *below* savers and is never significant.

## Key evidence

**Same-wave cross-section (BMI1989) — labelled cross-sectional association**
| exposure | unadj (n=10,410) | core (9,012) | +financial (6,875) | full (4,569) | full + BMI1981 (4,534) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| tp_ord | +0.308 (.039) | +0.216 (.043) | +0.253 (.051) | **+0.230 (.061)** p=1.6e-4 | **+0.096 (.041)** p=0.020 (**−58%**) |
| tp_high | +0.630 (.091) | +0.468 (.098) | +0.452 (.111) | +0.436 (.133) p=0.001 | +0.200 (.090) p=0.025 (**−54%**) |
| tp_cat3 (no-savings dropped) | +0.299 (.059) | +0.290 (.062) | +0.227 (.068) | +0.209 (.080) p=0.009 | +0.110 (.054) p=0.042 (−47%) |
| save_ratio (low = high TP) | −0.345 (.411) | −0.632 (.417) | −0.457 (.432) | −0.297 (.490) p=0.55 | −0.576 (.351) p=0.10 (null) |

Adjusted marginal means (full controls, n=4,569): saver 24.61 [24.39, 24.83] → no-change 24.87 → dis-saver 25.04 → no-savings 25.33 [25.01, 25.65] — monotone; with lagged BMI1981 the spread compresses to 24.78 → 25.05.

**Prospective (BMI1992 | BMI1989, attrition-fragile):** unadjusted +0.406 (n=8,498) → fully adjusted +0.063 (SE .036, p=0.082, n=3,861); tp_high +0.126 (p=0.099); 3-cat +0.050 (p=0.27); obese92 logit OR 1.15/step (p=0.023). ΔBMI1989→92 +0.057 (p=0.12). **Attrition:** 37.1% of the 1989 pool retained; cohort mix in the 1992 model 63.8% non-black/non-Hisp vs 57.3% in the pool (Hispanic 18.9% vs 26.0%); cohort post-stratification weights (0.90/1.38/0.97) give +0.065 (p=0.077) — composition-shifted but not overturned. Δweight 1981→1989 +0.59 lb/step (p=0.024) is reported as **reverse-time** (exposure posterior to the weight change), not causal.

**Is the 'no savings' stratum doing all the work? No, but it is the largest piece.** Fully adjusted category contrasts vs saver: dis-saver +0.43 (p=0.007), no-change +0.26 (p=0.19), no-savings +0.72 (p=0.0005). Dropping 'no savings' keeps +0.209 (p=0.009); the dis-saver-vs-saver contrast alone is +0.42 (p=0.009). The 'no savings' group is also by far the poorest (median 1985 wealth $300 vs $4,300 for savers; median 1989 income $12.5k vs $34k), yet its gap is *not* confined to asset-poor households (+0.48, p=0.018 where wealth>0; +0.39, p=0.39 where ≤0; interaction p=0.93). After lagged BMI1981 neither dis-saver (+0.12, p=0.22) nor no-savings (+0.16, p=0.21) remains significant — so the hypothesis wording is explicitly associational.

**Heterogeneity:** unadjusted r = +0.133 women vs +0.008 men; fully adjusted +0.299 (p=0.0015) vs +0.170 (p=0.025); both prospective estimates null (women +0.052, men +0.068). Optional class-percentile spec (~40%): +0.234 (p=0.004, n=2,647).

**Units/QC (metadata wrong, verified in data):** weights are **pounds** (median 140/158/165; 1981 sex means 161/129), height-1981 is **feet×100+inches** (400–611; v mod 100 never >11) while height-1985 is plain inches — decoded means agree (67.0 vs 67.1 in, r=0.934, median diff 0); person-mean height used; ASVAB "Z scores" are ~500/100 scores, re-standardised. Value-level invalidation counts: height81 11, height85 8, w81 1, w89 11, w92 0, BMI 1/11/4; sentinels put-in 8,192,797 (10), took-out 9,999,996 (20) → missing; income-1989 top-code 1,057,448 (167) winsorised (bounds −0.645/+0.395) before the ratio. **No rows deleted by QC** — only values, so n is driven solely by listwise control availability (ladder above).

**Missing data:** listwise headline + ladder; savings codes 3/4 → structural $0 (4,785 rows), 445 code-1/2 rows with sentinel/absent amounts kept missing. Sensitivities impute **controls only**: missing-indicator+median → +0.168 (n=10,410); stochastic chained-equation (MICE-style, M=10) → +0.166 (SD across imputations 0.007), sitting between listwise full-adjusted (+0.230) and prior-BMI-adjusted (+0.096). Exposure and outcomes never imputed.

## Assumptions
- Proxy validity: savings direction mixes preference with income shocks, liquidity needs, asset purchases and spouse behaviour (marital status absent); it is treated throughout as a behavioural present-orientation proxy, not a discount rate.
- Pound/feet-inches decodes and the code-3/4 structural-zero recode (approved); weights are unweighted (no panel weights in the extract).
- Net-saving ratio is only ~21% populated → robustness column only.

## Limitations
- Single savings wave: no repeated exposure, no person fixed effects; same-wave exposure window ends at the interview that measures BMI, so BMI1989 estimates are simultaneity-bound by construction.
- Prospective model loses 63% of the pool, over-represents the non-black/non-Hispanic cohort; the +0.063 is marginal and its CI includes zero.
- Lagged-BMI1981 models drop to n≈4,534 (36%) and are themselves selective; residual confounding (health, diet, smoking, marital status — none in the 61 columns) is unaddressed.
- Class rank/size covers 44% and had 2 rank>class-size records; used only in the labelled optional spec.
- BMI from self-reported height/weight (73% of weights are multiples of 5 lb) → heaping/measurement error; unit decodes are inference from distributions, though rank relations are insensitive to them.

payload.hypothesis: Higher present-oriented financial behaviour is associated with higher adiposity in NLSY79, but the association is mostly concurrent rather than prospective: measured as a savings-based present-orientation proxy (1989 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview', ordered put-more-in < no-change < took-more-out < no-savings, plus the dis-save/no-savings binary and a net-saving-to-income ratio), it predicts BMI1989 monotonically (mean BMI 24.54 / 24.97 / 25.14 / 25.50; obesity 10.1% / 11.6% / 13.0% / 15.6%; fully adjusted +0.23 BMI units per step, p=0.0002; +0.44 for dis-save-or-no-savings, about 0.1 SD or 1.3 kg), yet holding 1981 body mass fixed removes 54-58% of that gradient (+0.10 per step, p=0.02) and the genuinely prospective 1992 outcome conditional on 1989 BMI is only marginal (+0.06 per step, p=0.08, n=3,861, attrition-fragile and shifted toward the non-black/non-Hispanic cohort). Because higher BMI in 1981 itself predicts more present-oriented saving behaviour in 1989 (+0.013 per BMI unit, p=0.003), the evidence is consistent with a reciprocal wealth/weight/preference process and supports an ASSOCIATION between savings-based present orientation and higher BMI - strongest in women and in the 'no savings' stratum - rather than a demonstrated causal effect of increased time preference on BMI.
payload.workflow: analysis/run_all.py executes: (1) build_dataset.py - unit decodes (weights lb->kg; height-1981 feet*100+inches -> inches; person-mean height 1981/1985), value-level sentinel/QC invalidation with counts at every cut, savings structural-zero recode (codes 3/4 -> net $0), top-code winsorisation of the net-saving/income ratio, covariate construction, completeness and attrition tables; (2) models.py - retention ladder, correlations, cross-sectional OLS (BMI1989) for 7 exposure variants x 4 control sets with sex splits, lagged-BMI1981 on/off comparison, prospective BMI1992|BMI1989, within-person change models, obesity logits, optional class-percentile spec, controls-only missing-data sensitivity; (3) diagnostics.py - adjusted marginal means, 'no savings' driver decomposition and asset-poverty interaction, reverse-causality probe from BMI1981, 1992 attrition composition + cohort post-stratification, stochastic chained-equation (MICE-style) imputation of controls only; (4) summary_table.py - Table A (BMI mean/median/obesity by savings group, overall and by sex) and Table B (59 specifications with n, beta, SE, CI, p, design label, pre-registered sign match). Outputs: analysis/full_report.txt, table_A_*.csv, table_B_*.csv, HYPOTHESIS.md.
payload.prereg_sign: positive (higher present-orientation -> higher BMI); matches in 54/59 specs and 100% of primary exposures (save_ratio negative as expected)
